title: Waiter
directAnswer: Generate the first q primes. Run q rounds: in round i, scan the current pile and split it into plates divisible by the i-th prime (pile B) and the rest (the next pile A). Pop B onto the answer after each round, then continue with A. After all q rounds, pop whatever remains in A onto the answer. Each round is a single linear partition — O(n·q) total.

remember.pattern: Iterative stack partition by successive primes
rules: Use the **i-th prime** (2, 3, 5, 7, …) as the divisor in round i — precompute the first q primes.
Each round splits the current pile into `B` (divisible) and `A` (not divisible), preserving the pile's order during the scan.
Empty `B` onto the answer by **popping** it (last pushed first) after each round.
The pile that feeds round i+1 is `A` from round i; never re-include the plates already routed to `B`.
After the final round, empty the remaining pile `A` by popping it too.
whenToUse: Repeatedly partition a pile by a sequence of criteria, emptying one part each round
Stack-based bucketing where order of removal (LIFO) defines the output
Problems pairing a number-theory generator (primes) with a stack workflow
Multi-pass filtering where each pass uses the leftovers of the previous
antiSignals: A single fixed divisor → one partition pass, no prime sequence needed
You need all prime factors of each plate → factorisation, not divisibility by the i-th prime
Output order is FIFO, not LIFO → use a queue and don't reverse on emit
remember.takeaway: Waiter is a disciplined loop: precompute primes, then each round partition the current pile by the next prime, pop the divisible part to the answer, and recurse on the rest. The only traps are using the right (i-th) prime per round and emitting each pile by popping (LIFO).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can compose a prime generator with a clean iterative stack-partitioning loop, and get the LIFO emit order right.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using the wrong prime in a round, re-processing the divisible plates, or emitting piles in the wrong (non-popped) order — and generating primes inefficiently.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Separate concerns: a small prime sieve, then a single-responsibility partition-and-emit loop. Note each round is O(n) and the emit is a stack pop, so the LIFO order is intrinsic.

problemStatement:
You are given `number`, a list of `n` integers representing a stack of plates (front of the list is processed first each round), and an integer `q`.

Process `q` rounds. In round `i` (1-indexed) use the `i`-th prime `p_i` (so `p_1 = 2`, `p_2 = 3`, …). Scan the current pile: plates divisible by `p_i` go to pile `B_i`, the rest to pile `A_i`. After the round, the plates in `B_i` are placed on the answer pile (removed top-first / popped). The next round operates on `A_i`. After all `q` rounds, the plates left in `A_q` are placed on the answer pile (popped).

Return the answer pile from bottom to top (the order in which plates were placed).
constraints: Generate exactly the first q prime numbers
understanding: Think of plates flowing through q sieve stages. Stage i keeps the plates divisible by the i-th prime (they leave the conveyor onto the answer) and passes the rest to stage i+1. Each stage empties its 'divisible' bucket onto the answer by popping, so the most recently added plate in that bucket lands first. Whatever survives all q stages is emptied last.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which divisor does each round use?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Round i uses the i-th prime: 2, then 3, then 5, and so on. We precompute the first q primes once.

clarifyingQuestions.question: In what order are the divisible plates added to the answer?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Each round's divisible pile B is emptied by popping (LIFO) — the last plate routed to B is placed on the answer first.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the next round see the divisible plates again?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Once a plate is routed to B in some round it leaves the workflow. Only the non-divisible pile A continues.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens to plates that survive all q rounds?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: After the last round, the remaining pile A is emptied onto the answer by popping, just like a B pile.

examples.explanation: Prime 2. Divisible: 4,6 → pop B → 6,4. Remaining 3,7,5 → pop A → 5,7,3. Answer: 6,4,5,7,3.
Round 1 (p=2): B=4,4 → pop → 4,4; A=3,3,9. Round 2 (p=3): all of 3,3,9 divisible → B=3,3,9 → pop → 9,3,3. No leftovers. Answer: 4,4,9,3,3.

approaches.name: Naive Prime Test Per Round (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Acceptable to start here, then note the prime generation should be sieved and the partition kept clean.

complexity.time: O(n·q + cost of finding q primes naively)

hints: Two sub-problems: (1) get the first q primes, (2) repeatedly partition the pile by each prime.
A simple way to get primes is trial division: test each candidate against all smaller primes up to its square root.
For each round, walk the current pile, bucket plates into divisible vs not, then empty the divisible bucket onto the answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each round scans up to n plates → O(n·q) for partitioning. Naive trial-division prime finding adds a separate cost; both are acceptable for the given limits but the prime part is the part most worth optimising.
approaches.explanation:
The structure is the same as the optimal — the only difference is how we obtain the primes.

**Finding primes by trial division.** Starting at 2, test each candidate for primality by dividing by every prime already found that is ≤ √candidate. Collect until we have q of them. This is simple and, for q up to ~1200 (the 1200th prime is under 10000), perfectly fast.

**Partition each round.** With the primes in hand, run q rounds. In round i, scan the current pile and append each plate either to `B` (divisible by `primes[i]`) or to `A` (not). Empty `B` onto the answer by popping, then set the current pile to `A`.

**Why it's a fine baseline.** The partition loop is already optimal at O(n) per round. The trial-division prime finder is the only mildly wasteful piece, and even that is well within limits. We present the sieve version as the cleaner alternative, but correctness is identical.
approaches.insight: The problem cleanly decomposes into 'generate primes' and 'partition by prime'. Keeping those two concerns separate makes the code obviously correct; the only real choice is sieve vs trial division for the primes.

approaches.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes + Partition Loop (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The clean answer: sieve the primes once, then the same O(n) partition per round.

complexity.time: O(n·q + L log log L) where L bounds the q-th prime

hints: Generating q primes is faster with a sieve than repeated trial division — sieve up to a bound that safely contains the q-th prime.
The q-th prime is below about q·(ln q + ln ln q); for the given limits a bound near 10⁵ is comfortably safe.
Then the workflow is unchanged: q rounds, each an O(n) partition, popping the divisible pile onto the answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The sieve over a bound L runs in O(L log log L). Each of the q rounds scans up to n plates → O(n·q). Space is the sieve array plus the piles.
approaches.explanation:
Same two-part structure, but generate the primes with a Sieve of Eratosthenes for speed and clarity.

**Choosing the sieve bound.** We need the first `q` primes. By the prime counting bound, the `q`-th prime is below roughly `q·(ln q + ln ln q)`. For `q ≤ 1200` a bound around `10⁵` is more than enough; in general compute a safe upper bound and sieve up to it, then take the first `q` primes found.

**The sieve.** Mark multiples of each prime starting from 2; the unmarked numbers are prime. Collect them in increasing order and keep the first `q`. This is the standard, cache-friendly way to enumerate small primes.

**The partition rounds.** Identical to the baseline: for round `i`, scan the current pile and bucket each plate into `B` (divisible by `primes[i]`) or `A` (not). Empty `B` onto the answer by popping, then continue with `A`. After the final round, empty `A`.

**Why popping gives the required order.** Each pile behaves as a stack: plates are pushed during the scan and popped onto the answer, so the last plate added to a pile is placed first. That LIFO behaviour is exactly the 'remove from the top' semantics the problem describes for emptying a pile onto the answer.
approaches.insight: The whole solution is two well-known building blocks wired in series: a sieve to produce primes, and a stack-partition loop to route plates. Recognising that 'empty the pile onto the answer' means a stack pop is what makes the output order fall out automatically — no manual reversing logic needed beyond popping.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Emitting a pile in the wrong order
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The problem removes plates from the top of a pile (LIFO). Appending a pile to the answer in scan order reverses the intended output; you must pop it.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for plate in b:
    answer.append(plate)   # scan order — wrong
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
while b:
    answer.append(b.pop()) # popped (LIFO) order — correct

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to flush the last pile
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Plates not divisible by any of the q primes survive every round and sit in the final pile A. If you stop after the loop without emptying A, those plates are missing from the answer.
